ripple_effect.name: Coup or abrupt regime change disrupting trade relationships

historical_precedents.event: Niger military coup
historical_precedents.what_happened: On 26 July 2023, General Abdourahamane Tchiani led the presidential guard in removing President Mohamed Bazoum and installed a military council. The regional bloc ECOWAS responded with an ultimatum, then sanctions including closed land and air borders, a no-fly zone on commercial flights, suspension of financial transactions, and asset freezes; Nigeria cut electricity supply to Niger on 2 August 2023.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The West African regional central bank cancelled a planned 30 billion CFA franc (about $51 million) bond issuance for Niger, and the World Bank suspended disbursements to the country. Niger is a significant global uranium exporter, and the coup raised questions over the operations of French nuclear fuel company Orano's mining activities there.

historical_precedents.event: Myanmar military coup
historical_precedents.what_happened: Senior General Min Aung Hlaing seized power on 1 February 2021, detaining civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi and other elected officials. The Biden administration imposed sanctions on military leaders on 11 February 2021 and froze $1 billion in Myanmar government assets held in the U.S.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Foreign direct investment into Myanmar fell 22% to $3.8 billion in fiscal year 2020, and major foreign investors withdrew: Japan's Kirin ended a $1.7 billion brewery joint venture, Thailand's Amata halted a $1 billion industrial zone project, and India's Adani Ports terminated a $127 million port investment. The Yangon Stock Exchange suspended trading, and property sales reportedly dropped by nearly 100%.

possibility_chains: A coup in a country that is a significant exporter of a specific commodity has historically raised questions about the continuity of that country's mining, energy, or agricultural exports, even when physical production is not immediately disrupted.
Coups have historically triggered sanctions and suspended aid or financing from regional blocs and international lenders, adding fiscal strain on top of the immediate political disruption.

Foreign companies operating in a country that experiences a coup have historically paused or withdrawn planned investment until the new government's posture toward existing contracts and foreign ownership becomes clearer.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Myanmar military coup (February 2021): Foreign direct investment into Myanmar fell 22% to $3.8 billion in fiscal year 2020, and major foreign investors withdrew: Japan's Kirin ended a $1.7 billion brewery joint venture, Thailand's Amata halted a $1 billion industrial zone project, and India's Adani Ports terminated a $127 million port investment. The Yangon Stock Exchange suspended trading, and property sales reportedly dropped by nearly 100%. A coup in a country that is a significant exporter of a specific commodity has historically raised questions about the continuity of that country's mining, energy, or agricultural exports, even when physical production is not immediately disrupted.

Sanctions targeting a major energy or commodity exporter have historically tightened global supply of that commodity, which has often (though not always, depending on how much other producers can offset the loss) pushed prices higher.

historical_precedents.event: Germany's 'Zeitenwende' defense policy shift
historical_precedents.what_happened: In a speech to the Bundestag on 27 February 2022, three days after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Chancellor Olaf Scholz announced a one-time €100 billion special fund to modernize Germany's armed forces and committed Germany to spending over 2% of GDP on defense, a NATO membership guideline Germany had not previously met. By 2024, Germany had reached NATO's 2%-of-GDP defense spending target.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The announcement marked a historic reversal of Germany's post-WWII restraint on military spending and was followed by German defense contractors reporting substantially higher order backlogs in subsequent years.

possibility_chains: A major security shock in a region has historically prompted neighboring or allied countries to announce sizable defense spending increases in the following weeks, even though actually building and delivering new military hardware has typically taken years.

Sustained higher defense spending commitments have historically boosted revenue and order backlogs for domestic and allied defense contractors, with the effect showing up in company earnings over subsequent quarters and years.

Countries that historically kept defense spending below alliance guidelines have, following a major rearmament announcement, faced years of budget and industrial-capacity planning to translate the announced spending into delivered equipment.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Germany's 'Zeitenwende' defense policy shift (February 2022 – 2024): The announcement marked a historic reversal of Germany's post-WWII restraint on military spending and was followed by German defense contractors reporting substantially higher order backlogs in subsequent years. A major security shock in a region has historically prompted neighboring or allied countries to announce sizable defense spending increases in the following weeks, even though actually building and delivering new military hardware has typically taken years.

linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Finland and Sweden's accession following Russia's invasion of Ukraine (2022–2024): Russia's Defense Ministry said Finland's accession significantly increased the risk of a wider conflict in Europe and doubled the length of NATO's border with Russia, while President Putin publicly dismissed the accessions as posing no direct threat to Russia; both new members proceeded with defense-spending commitments tied to NATO membership. linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty signing and collapse (1987–2019): Both the U.S. and Russia became free to develop and deploy previously-banned intermediate-range missile systems; Russia subsequently advanced hypersonic and Kalibr missile programs, and the collapse renewed debate over the future of New START, the last remaining major U.S.-Russia arms control agreement. historical_precedents.event: Galwan Valley clash between India and China
historical_precedents.what_happened: Indian and Chinese soldiers engaged in hand-to-hand combat, no firearms were used per long-standing agreements governing the disputed border, at Patrolling Point 14 in the Galwan Valley along the disputed Line of Actual Control. Border incidents between countries with significant bilateral trade or investment ties have historically prompted the affected government to restrict specific categories of trade or investment, such as apps, technology, or particular imports, from the other country, sometimes lasting years after the initial incident.

States involved in a border clash have historically exercised restraint from escalating to full-scale conflict even after fatalities, relying instead on established de-escalation and disengagement protocols.

ripple_effect.name: African swine fever outbreak collapses China's pork supply

historical_precedents.event: African swine fever spreads across China's pig herd
historical_precedents.what_happened: China's first confirmed case of African swine fever was reported in Liaoning province in August 2018 (with more than 38,000 hogs culled within the first two weeks); within about eight months the disease had spread to every region of China. China's pig population fell by almost 100 million head compared with the previous year — roughly a quarter of the global pig population affected. The disease also spread through Southeast Asia, reaching Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, and Vietnam.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The resulting pork supply shortage pushed China to sharply increase pork imports, and European pork prices reached a six-year high as international demand rose to help fill the gap left by China's collapsed domestic production.

possibility_chains: A livestock disease outbreak in the world's largest producer/consumer of a given meat has historically reshaped global trade flows for that commodity, pulling imports from exporting countries and raising prices in those export markets too.

Countries hit by a major livestock epidemic have historically accelerated biosecurity investment and herd-rebuilding programs, a process that has typically taken multiple years to restore pre-outbreak production levels.

A large, sudden loss of one protein source has historically shifted consumer demand toward substitute proteins (e.g. poultry, beef, or soy-based products) in the affected country, with knock-on price effects in those markets.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: African swine fever spreads across China's pig herd (August 2018 – 2019): The resulting pork supply shortage pushed China to sharply increase pork imports, and European pork prices reached a six-year high as international demand rose to help fill the gap left by China's collapsed domestic production. A livestock disease outbreak in the world's largest producer/consumer of a given meat has historically reshaped global trade flows for that commodity, pulling imports from exporting countries and raising prices in those export markets too.

linked_playbooks.name: Avian influenza outbreak drives poultry and egg price shock
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) forces mass culling of U.S. egg-laying hens (2022 onward): The mass culling sharply reduced the U.S. egg-laying flock and was followed by 'skyrocketing' egg prices, a pattern that recurred with further culling waves in subsequent years; egg producers such as Cal-Maine later faced scrutiny, including litigation over pricing coordination between 2022 and 2025, during the shortage period. A major livestock disease outbreak that forces large-scale culling has historically produced protein-specific price spikes (e.g. eggs or poultry) within months, distinct from broader crop-driven food inflation.

linked_playbooks.name: Major tariff escalation / trade war
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan (September 2010 – 2011): China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). The U.S. filed a WTO case in 2012; the WTO ruled against China in 2014, and China dropped its export quotas in 2015 — but the episode had already pushed Japan and other importers to diversify sourcing and boost recycling. New tariffs have historically raised the cost of the affected imported goods, at least part of which has often been passed on to consumers or absorbed as lower profit margins by importers.

historical_precedents.event: Philippines v. China Permanent Court of Arbitration case

historical_precedents.event: UK four-day week pilot (4 Day Week Global / Autonomy)
historical_precedents.what_happened: 61 companies employing about 2,900 workers across the UK trialed a "100-80-100" model — 100% of pay for 80% of the working time, in exchange for a commitment to maintain 100% productivity — with the trial overseen by researchers from Boston College, Oxford, and Cambridge alongside the think tank Autonomy.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Revenue at participating companies rose more than a third compared with the same period a year earlier, staff turnover fell, and over 90% of participating companies chose to continue with the four-day format after the trial ended, with 86% saying they planned to keep it permanently.

historical_precedents.market_impact: Researchers found productivity held steady or improved at most participating workplaces alongside large gains in reported wellbeing, and the trials' results fed into subsequent union contract negotiations — by the early 2020s an estimated 86% of Iceland's wage-earning workforce had secured permanently shortened hours or the right to negotiate them.

historical_precedents.event: Nigeria's 'Occupy Nigeria' fuel subsidy protests
historical_precedents.what_happened: The government removed Nigeria's longstanding petrol subsidy on January 1, 2012, roughly doubling pump prices from 65 to at least 141 naira per litre; nationwide strikes and protests followed for nearly two weeks (January 2–14) across Lagos, Abuja, Kano, and other cities, with trade unions announcing an indefinite strike from January 9.
historical_precedents.market_impact: About 16 people were killed in clashes between protesters and police, and the government partially walked back the increase before the standoff ended.

historical_precedents.event: Ecuador's Decree 883 fuel subsidy removal and reversal
historical_precedents.what_happened: President Lenín Moreno eliminated 40-year-old fuel subsidies on October 1, 2019 as part of an IMF-linked austerity package addressing $64 billion in debt, roughly doubling diesel prices and raising petrol prices about 30%; indigenous groups (CONAIE), transport workers, and students staged nationwide protests from October 3–14.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The unrest left 8 dead, over 1,300 injured, and nearly 1,200 detained; President Moreno reversed the policy by signing Decree 894 on October 14, 2019, restoring subsidies to previous levels after a televised agreement with indigenous leaders.

historical_precedents.event: Global burden-of-disease estimate for bacterial antimicrobial resistance
historical_precedents.what_happened: A global analysis found bacterial antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was directly responsible for an estimated 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019 and was associated with roughly 4.95 million deaths that year overall, with Sub-Saharan Africa (23.7 per 100,000) and South Asia (21.5 per 100,000) recording the highest death rates.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The World Bank projected that, left unaddressed, AMR could raise global healthcare costs by roughly $1 trillion and cause annual global economic losses of $1–3.4 trillion by 2030, while the WHO has cited projections warning of up to 10 million deaths a year globally by 2050 without intervention.

historical_precedents.event: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) EU/EEA burden estimate
historical_precedents.what_happened: ECDC documented 671,689 infections in the EU and European Economic Area caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria in 2015.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Those infections were estimated to have caused 33,110 deaths that year — a toll comparable to the combined burden of several other major infectious diseases in the EU — and contributed to sustained EU-level policy pushes for new antibiotic development incentives given weak commercial returns on new antibiotics held in reserve rather than sold at volume.

possibility_chains: Weak commercial incentives for new antibiotic R&D — since new antibiotics are typically held in reserve for resistant cases rather than sold at high volume — have historically led several large drugmakers to exit antibiotic development entirely.

ripple_effect.name: Critical minerals supply shock for clean energy

historical_precedents.event: Indonesia's nickel ore export ban
historical_precedents.what_happened: Indonesia, the world's largest nickel producer (accounting for roughly 48% of global mined supply as of 2022), banned exports of unprocessed nickel ore starting January 2020 — two years earlier than a previously scheduled 2022 deadline — to force foreign investment into domestic smelting and, eventually, battery-grade nickel processing for EV batteries.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The announcement of the accelerated ban pushed world nickel prices up about 8.8% to a five-year high; the policy has since driven a large buildout of Indonesian nickel-processing capacity, much of it financed by Chinese investment, reshaping where a key EV battery input is refined.

historical_precedents.event: China's dominance of rare-earth processing and use of export restrictions
historical_precedents.what_happened: China has supplied around 90% of global rare-earth-element demand in recent years and has periodically restricted rare-earth exports since around 2010; during renewed trade tensions with the US, China imposed new restrictions on exports of several heavy rare earths and rare-earth magnets on 2 April 2025.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Rare-earth magnets are a critical input for wind turbine generators and electric-vehicle motors as well as defense systems; the restrictions prompted the US and other countries to accelerate efforts to develop non-Chinese rare-earth mining and processing capacity, and the US moved to bar Chinese-origin rare-earth metals and magnets from defense procurement starting January 2027.

possibility_chains: A single country's dominance of mining or processing for a specific clean-energy input (nickel, cobalt, lithium, or rare earths) has historically given it outsized leverage over global battery, wind-turbine, or EV-motor supply chains, regardless of where the final products are assembled.

Export restrictions on a concentrated critical mineral have historically taken years, not months, for importing countries to offset through new mining or processing investment elsewhere, given how long permitting and plant construction takes.

Higher critical-mineral costs have historically fed through into the price of EV batteries, wind turbines, and other clean-energy hardware, at least temporarily slowing the pace of cost declines in those technologies.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: China's dominance of rare-earth processing and use of export restrictions (2010 onward, escalating through 2025): Rare-earth magnets are a critical input for wind turbine generators and electric-vehicle motors as well as defense systems; the restrictions prompted the US and other countries to accelerate efforts to develop non-Chinese rare-earth mining and processing capacity, and the US moved to bar Chinese-origin rare-earth metals and magnets from defense procurement starting January 2027. linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: US Section 201 tariffs on imported solar cells and modules (January 2018): The tariffs contributed to the cancellation or scaling-back of some planned US solar installation projects in the near term and slowed hiring on the installation side of the industry, while domestic US solar cell manufacturing capacity increased from about 1.8 gigawatts in 2017 to at least 3.4 gigawatts in 2018; by 2019 the broader US solar industry had resumed growth as underlying panel costs continued to fall. Tariffs on imported solar components have historically raised near-term installation costs and slowed project timelines in the importing country's downstream solar industry (installers and developers), even while incentivizing new domestic manufacturing capacity.

linked_playbooks.name: Semiconductor export controls
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Japan's export controls on South Korea (July 2019): Samsung and SK Hynix, which together accounted for roughly 72% of global DRAM output at the time, faced procurement uncertainty; Samsung reported a 12.4% year-on-year operating profit decline in Q3 2019, partly linked to the disruption. linked_playbooks.name: Major tariff escalation / trade war
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan (September 2010 – 2011): China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). The U.S. filed a WTO case in 2012; the WTO ruled against China in 2014, and China dropped its export quotas in 2015 — but the episode had already pushed Japan and other importers to diversify sourcing and boost recycling. New tariffs have historically raised the cost of the affected imported goods, at least part of which has often been passed on to consumers or absorbed as lower profit margins by importers.

historical_precedents.what_happened: A prolonged standoff in Congress over raising the federal debt ceiling was resolved with the Budget Control Act, signed August 1–2, 2011, which paired a $900 billion debt ceiling increase with $917 billion in spending cuts over a decade.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Days later, on August 5, 2011, S&P downgraded the US credit rating from AAA to AA+ for the first time in history, and major stock indices fell as much as 4% in the days around the downgrade — the largest drop since July 2009 — while crude oil and gold prices also fell amid broad-based selling.

historical_precedents.event: 2023 US debt ceiling crisis
historical_precedents.what_happened: The US hit its debt ceiling on January 19, 2023, prompting the Treasury to use 'extraordinary measures' as Republicans and Democrats deadlocked over spending conditions; President Biden and Speaker McCarthy reached a deal on May 27, 2023, and the resulting Fiscal Responsibility Act was signed into law by June 3, 2023.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The act suspended the debt limit until January 1, 2025; weeks later, on August 1, 2023, Fitch downgraded the US credit rating from AAA to AA+, citing repeated brinkmanship over the debt ceiling among its reasons.

Extended standoffs have historically weighed on consumer and business confidence surveys in the weeks leading up to a deadline, even without an actual default occurring.

ripple_effect.name: Government austerity program (spending cuts and tax rises)

historical_precedents.event: UK austerity programme under Chancellor George Osborne
historical_precedents.what_happened: Following his June 2010 budget, the Conservative-led coalition pursued roughly £110 billion in combined spending cuts and tax increases aimed at eliminating the structural deficit, including over £30 billion in welfare cuts, a 2011–2013 public sector pay freeze, and reductions that cut local government funding by an estimated 60% over the decade.
historical_precedents.market_impact: About 220,000 local authority jobs were eliminated and nearly 800 public libraries closed between 2010 and 2020; a 2017 University College London study published in BMJ Open found that annual health-funding growth fell from 3.8% in the 2000s to 0.41% after 2010, and researchers linked the slowdown in health and social care spending to a rise in mortality-rate growth over the same period.

historical_precedents.event: Canada's 1995 federal budget under Finance Minister Paul Martin
historical_precedents.what_happened: Facing a $30 billion federal deficit, Canada's budget cut program spending by a planned 18.9% by 1997–98, eliminated dozens of federal agencies and business subsidies (including a $560 million annual rail subsidy), and merged two separate federal transfer programs into a single, reduced Canada Health and Social Transfer block grant to the provinces.
historical_precedents.market_impact: By shrinking the federal transfer, the reform shifted fiscal pressure onto provincial governments, which had to make their own cuts to health and social assistance spending to absorb the reduced federal contribution.

possibility_chains: Government austerity programs that cut public sector employment have historically taken years to fully play out in local labor markets, as affected workers and the local businesses that served them adjust gradually rather than all at once.

Cuts concentrated in health and social services have historically been linked by researchers to slower improvement (or reversal) in public health outcomes, though isolating austerity's specific contribution from other factors has remained a subject of academic debate.

Federal-level austerity that reduces transfers to regional or local governments has historically pushed the political and fiscal burden of further cuts down to those lower levels of government, which have fewer tools (such as currency issuance or unlimited borrowing) to absorb the shortfall.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Canada's 1995 federal budget under Finance Minister Paul Martin (1995): By shrinking the federal transfer, the reform shifted fiscal pressure onto provincial governments, which had to make their own cuts to health and social assistance spending to absorb the reduced federal contribution. Government austerity programs that cut public sector employment have historically taken years to fully play out in local labor markets, as affected workers and the local businesses that served them adjust gradually rather than all at once.

linked_playbooks.name: IMF bailout or rescue program for a sovereign
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Sri Lanka's IMF Extended Fund Facility after its 2022 default (2022–2024): The program aimed to raise Sri Lanka's tax-to-GDP ratio from 8.1% in 2021 to 15% by 2025, but the accompanying austerity coincided with unemployment rising from 5.7% to 8.3% between 2022 and 2023. linked_playbooks.name: Eurozone periphery sovereign bond crisis
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Mario Draghi's 'whatever it takes' pledge (July 2012): The pledge is widely credited as the turning point in the crisis, prompting a steady decline in borrowing costs for Spain, Italy, and other periphery economies in the following months, even though the OMT program itself was never actually activated. Rising bond yields in one eurozone member has historically raised borrowing costs in other members seen as having similar debt vulnerabilities, a contagion dynamic distinct from a single-country crisis.

linked_playbooks.name: Pension/retirement-age reform triggers unrest
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: France's 2010 pension reform under President Sarkozy (September–October 2010): The strikes shut down all twelve of mainland France's oil refineries, leaving roughly one in four fuel stations dry nationwide, and cancelled about half of long-distance trains and up to 50% of flights at major airports before the government passed the reform largely unchanged. linked_playbooks.name: Major municipal or county bankruptcy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Jefferson County, Alabama bankruptcy (November 2011 – December 2013): The county cut its government workforce by more than 700 employees by May 2012, and the bankruptcy court wrote off more than $1.4 billion of the debt before the county emerged from bankruptcy in December 2013. ripple_effect.name: Central bank interest rate hikes

historical_precedents.event: U.S. Federal Reserve's fastest rate-hiking cycle in decades
historical_precedents.what_happened: The Fed raised its benchmark interest rate from near zero to over 5% in about 16 months, responding to the highest inflation in roughly 40 years.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The average 30-year U.S. mortgage rate roughly doubled from around 3% to over 7%, home sales slowed sharply, and high-growth technology stocks — more sensitive to rate changes — fell substantially more than the broader market in 2022.

historical_precedents.event: Fed Chair Paul Volcker's rate hikes to break double-digit inflation
historical_precedents.what_happened: The Fed raised interest rates to nearly 20% to bring runaway inflation under control.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The policy triggered a deep recession and a sharp rise in unemployment before inflation was brought down over the following years.

historical_precedents.event: European Central Bank rate hikes under Jean-Claude Trichet
historical_precedents.what_happened: The ECB raised its benchmark rate twice in 2011 (to 1.25% in April, then 1.5% in July) to fight headline inflation, even as the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis was worsening — Portugal's debt was downgraded to junk the same day as the July hike.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Peripheral Eurozone bond yields (Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece) surged in the following months as the debt crisis deepened; the hikes are widely regarded in hindsight as a policy mistake, and the ECB reversed course with cuts in November and December 2011 after Mario Draghi succeeded Trichet as president — a case where a rate-hike decision, unlike the Fed episodes above, is broadly seen as having worsened rather than merely responded to a crisis.

ripple_effect.name: Broad-based voluntary quits wave / labor shortage

historical_precedents.event: The "Great Resignation" in the United States
historical_precedents.what_happened: A record 47 million Americans voluntarily quit their jobs in 2021 alone, with the monthly quits rate reaching roughly 3% — a level never before recorded since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking it in December 2000 (prior peak 2.4%) — as workers cited wage stagnation, burnout, and inflexible return-to-office policies; food-service quit rates hit 6.8% in October 2021, and about 2.4 million Baby Boomers retired earlier than pre-pandemic trends would have predicted.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Employers responded with the fastest wage growth in two decades — 4.5% year-over-year in December 2021 — while hospitality, healthcare, and education faced acute staffing shortages that pushed many businesses to accelerate investment in automation and self-service technology; quits rates did not return to pre-pandemic 2019 norms until mid-2023.

possibility_chains: A sustained period of unusually high voluntary quits has historically coincided with faster wage growth, as employers compete harder to retain and attract staff in a tight labor market.

Sector-specific quit spikes (hospitality, retail, healthcare during the Great Resignation) have historically prompted employers in those specific sectors to accelerate automation investment, a shift that has typically outlasted the labor shortage that originally motivated it.

A broad wave of voluntary job-switching has historically correlated with a period of unusually strong worker bargaining power, which employer-side surveys and union-organizing activity have both tended to pick up on with a lag of several months.

linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Starbucks Workers United organizing campaign (December 2021 – ongoing): By mid-2026 over 15,000 workers across 706 Starbucks locations had voted to unionize; Starbucks contested the campaign through captive-audience meetings, firing organizers (leading to repeated NLRB findings of "egregious and widespread" labor-law violations, over 80 documented claims), closing some unionized stores including all locations in Ithaca, NY, and a Supreme Court case that made NLRB-ordered reinstatement of fired workers harder to obtain. linked_playbooks.name: Minimum wage policy shift
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Seattle becomes the first major US city to adopt a $15 minimum wage (2014–2019): University of Washington and other researchers studying Seattle's rollout found no measurable decline in overall employment as the wage floor rose, making Seattle a frequently cited case study in the broader minimum-wage debate. A minimum wage increase in one large city or state has historically prompted advocacy campaigns citing it as precedent for similar increases elsewhere, spreading policy change faster than pure economic modeling alone would predict.

historical_precedents.event: Puerto Rico's government-debt crisis and PROMESA restructuring
historical_precedents.what_happened: Puerto Rico's bonds were downgraded to junk status in February 2014, and Governor García Padilla declared the roughly $74 billion in bond debt (plus $49 billion in unfunded pension liabilities) 'not payable' on June 28, 2015; after Puerto Rico missed a $422 million payment on May 1, 2016, Congress passed PROMESA, which President Obama signed June 30, 2016, creating a federal oversight board with authority over the territory's budget and debt restructuring.

signals.headline: Tikoduadua Calls for Justice for Nuclear Test Victims

ripple_effect.name: Nuclear or long-range missile test triggering international sanctions

historical_precedents.event: North Korea's sixth nuclear test and ICBM tests
historical_precedents.what_happened: North Korea conducted its sixth and largest nuclear test on 3 September 2017, with seismic activity assessed at roughly 10 times more powerful than its previous test and an estimated yield of around 250 kilotons; the U.S. Geological Survey recorded a magnitude 6.3 event. Earlier that year, North Korea also test-fired intercontinental ballistic missiles on 4 July and 28 July 2017 that analysts assessed were capable of reaching the continental United States.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2375 on 11 September 2017, capping North Korea's refined petroleum imports (initially 500,000 barrels over three months, then 2 million barrels annually), banning all textile exports (an estimated $800 million annual revenue loss), and phasing out visas for North Korean overseas workers (estimated to cost North Korea another $500 million a year) — among the most restrictive sanctions the Council had imposed on the country to that point.

possibility_chains: A major nuclear or long-range missile test has historically prompted the UN Security Council to negotiate new sanctions resolutions in the following days to weeks, though the scope of sanctions has depended on securing agreement from all five permanent members, including the tested country's key trading partners.

Sanctions that target a specific export sector, such as textiles, or a labor-export revenue stream have historically been calibrated to cut off specific, identifiable sources of foreign currency earnings for the sanctioned government.

Repeated missile and nuclear tests over time have historically produced diminishing market and diplomatic reaction with each subsequent test, as neighboring countries and investors adjust to a higher baseline level of tension.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: North Korea's sixth nuclear test and ICBM tests (2017): The UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2375 on 11 September 2017, capping North Korea's refined petroleum imports (initially 500,000 barrels over three months, then 2 million barrels annually), banning all textile exports (an estimated $800 million annual revenue loss), and phasing out visas for North Korean overseas workers (estimated to cost North Korea another $500 million a year) — among the most restrictive sanctions the Council had imposed on the country to that point. A major nuclear or long-range missile test has historically prompted the UN Security Council to negotiate new sanctions resolutions in the following days to weeks, though the scope of sanctions has depended on securing agreement from all five permanent members, including the tested country's key trading partners.

linked_playbooks.name: Major arms control treaty withdrawal or collapse
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty signing and collapse (1987–2019): Both the U.S. and Russia became free to develop and deploy previously-banned intermediate-range missile systems; Russia subsequently advanced hypersonic and Kalibr missile programs, and the collapse renewed debate over the future of New START, the last remaining major U.S.-Russia arms control agreement. The collapse of a major arms control treaty has historically prompted both sides to resume or accelerate development of previously-restricted weapons systems, a process that has typically unfolded over years given weapons-development timelines.

linked_playbooks.name: Sanctions imposed on a major economy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: International sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program (2010s): Iranian oil exports fell sharply, though global oil prices were also affected by supply from other producers filling the gap; Iran's own currency and economy experienced significant strain during the most restrictive sanctions periods. Sanctions targeting a major energy or commodity exporter have historically tightened global supply of that commodity, which has often (though not always, depending on how much other producers can offset the loss) pushed prices higher.
